analysis.one_liner: Bans bank overdraft and bounced-check fees during declared disasters like the coronavirus emergency.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 2020 and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, the bill never received a committee hearing or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During a federally declared major disaster or emergency, the bill would make it illegal for banks to charge overdraft fees or non-sufficient fund fees on checking accounts, and to report overdrafts to credit bureaus. It would remain in force until 120 days after the disaster's incident period ends. The goal was to stop banks from collecting billions in penalty fees from customers whose finances were disrupted by the COVID-19 emergency. The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Checking-account customers who overdraw their accounts, who are disproportionately low- and moderate-income households living paycheck to paycheck. During the COVID-19 emergency they would have kept the money that banks would otherwise collect as flat fees per overdraft transaction, and avoided credit-report damage from overdraft use.

how_it_helps.text: During the covered period, no depository institution could assess a non-sufficient fund fee or an overdraft coverage fee on any transaction, including ATM withdrawals, one-time debit card purchases, checks, or automatic recurring payments [S3].
Banks could not report a consumer's overdraft use to any consumer reporting agency during the covered period, protecting the customer's credit record [S3].

The bill's findings state that banks aggressively push consumers into the most expensive overdraft option, charge high flat fees even on small-dollar transactions, impose multiple fees in a single day, and add daily fees while an account stays overdrawn, burdening low- and moderate-income consumers [S3].

The prohibition applies during any federally declared major disaster or emergency and stays in effect until 120 days after the incident period ends, so it would have covered the COVID-19 emergency nationwide [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Depository institutions — banks, thrifts, and credit unions — which would forgo overdraft and non-sufficient fund fee revenue during the covered period. Overdraft fees are a multi-billion-dollar annual revenue stream concentrated at large banks. Some banks might respond by declining overdraft transactions more often rather than covering them for free, which could leave a customer's payment unpaid.

drawbacks.text: Overdraft coverage is short-term credit that banks provide; if they cannot charge for it, some banks may simply decline transactions instead, leaving customers with a card that does not work or a bill that goes unpaid [S3].
The relief is temporary: the ban ends 120 days after a disaster's incident period closes, and the fee practices themselves remain legal in normal times [S3].
The bill covers overdraft fees but leaves other bank fees untouched, and it does not address the underlying shortage of funds that causes overdrafts in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households hit by a disaster, the benefit is direct: penalty fees of $30 or more per transaction, sometimes several per day, would stop being deducted from already-stressed accounts, and overdrafts would not damage credit reports. The main cost falls on banks, whose overdraft revenue is real but whose costs of covering small overdrafts are modest. The honest weakness is that a fee ban may change bank behavior — more declined payments rather than covered overdrafts — and the relief ends when the disaster period does, leaving the underlying fee structure untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on March 22, 2020, referred to the Senate Banking Committee the same day, and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on March 22, 2020, 'for himself and Mr. Brown,' three days after the President had declared a nationwide emergency over the coronavirus [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where it remained; the action history shows no further action of any kind [S5].
It drew a single cosponsor in the Senate and was never scheduled for committee consideration or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other depository institutions came out ahead: they kept collecting overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees on customers overdrawn during the pandemic emergency, a revenue stream the bill would have suspended. Consumers who overdraw accounts during disasters gained nothing from this Congress, though later regulators and banks adopted some voluntary pandemic-era fee relief on their own.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 22, 2020 to ban overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees during declared disasters.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OH), cosponsor and senior member of the Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor; the bill was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Brown.'

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on March 22, 2020; no hearing, markup, or report followed for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the Republican-led Senate Banking Committee took no action on the bill; no vote was ever held, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: Overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees are a major fee-revenue stream, built on flat charges per transaction that fall hardest on low-balance customers. The bill would have suspended that revenue during disasters and barred credit-reporting of overdrafts, so the industry's interest ran directly against the consumers the bill protected.
